newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech govt announces economic stimulus package.
newsitem.headline: Czech govt announces economic stimulus package.

text.p: The Czech government on Wednesday announced its package of proposals to stimulate the economy, limiting public sector wage growth, cutting budget expenditures and reforming the capital markets.

A government statement said that monetary policy changes, including any exchange rate measures, were up to the central bank. It added that the current +/-7.5 percent fluctuation band for fixing the crown appeared to be sufficient.

The statement said that the government would cut 25.5 billion crowns from state budget expenditures, and limit public sector wage growth to 7.3 percent, year-on-year, from an originally planned 11.9 percent.
The 1997 budget, approved by parliament in December, calls for balanced expenditures and revenues of 549.1 billion crowns.

In announcing the measures, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said there would be cuts of 20 percent in all investment expenditures, except in the defence and transport sectors, where the cut would be eight percent. He added the slowdown in wage growth would also apply to state-held firms.
Klaus said that the trade deficit, which hit a record 160.3 billion crowns for 1996 and has shown no signs of slowing in 1997, called for action.

He said the government would implement an import curbs programme, requiring firms to place funds into a non-interest earning account at the central bank to cover a portion of the goods they are importing.

The statement said the charge would be either 20 percent or 60 percent, and apply only to foodstuffs and consumer goods. Klaus said that Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy would finalise details of the import deposit programme on Friday. The programme is only to last one year, the statement added.

The statement also calls for a speeding up of the privatisation of companies and banks using "combinations of standard privatisation methods which will ensure an optimal combination of speed, (financial) proceeds and sensitivity to the effects of privatisation".

"Above all, (the process should find) responsible owners of privatised property with a long term interest in prosperity of the companies...Proposals shall be presented by the Ministry of Finance and relevant departments by the end of May," it said.
The statement said that the government wouldpropose a corporate tax cut to 35 percent from 39 percent effective january 1, 1998.
The statement also said that personal tax brackets and rates would be raised to help boost revenues, as well as an increase in excise taxes on goods such as alcohol and tobacco products.

To help bring about more tansparency in the capital markets, long-criticsied as rife with insider trading and poor regulation, the government said the Finance Ministry would submit a proposal by May to create an independent market watchdog similar to the U.S. Securities Exchange Commission.
